records.title: Accelerated Intermittent Theta-Burst Stimulation for the Treatment of Alcohol Use Disorder: A Randomized Sham-Controlled Study With Six-Month Follow-Up.
records.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Accelerated intermittent theta-burst stimulation (a-iTBS) is a novel rTMS protocol increasingly used for mental disorders, but its application in alcohol use disorder (AUD) remains early. This exploratory sham-controlled study evaluated a 50-session a-iTBS protocol for AUD.
METHODS: Sixty-one male AUD inpatients were randomized to receive traditional iTBS (once daily, 600 pulse/session), a-iTBS (5 sessions/day, 3000 pulses/day), or sham iTBS. Treatments were administered on 10 weekdays (Monday to Friday over 2 weeks) and targeted the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. The primary outcome was the change in craving. The alcohol relapse behavior, emotional symptoms, and sleep quality were evaluated pre-/post-intervention.
RESULTS: Group showed no significant main effect on craving percentage change. The a-iTBS group showed a higher response rate and earlier response onset than the s-iTBS group, whereas no significant differences existed between a-iTBS and iTBS, or iTBS and s-iTBS. No intergroup differences were detected for mood and sleep indicators. At the 6-month follow-up, participants receiving a-iTBS achieved longer abstinence duration than those given s-iTBS. Exploratory logistic regression indicated that baseline GAD-7 scores and treatment group were associated with treatment response.
CONCLUSIONS: Although the primary craving outcome did not differ significantly among groups, a-iTBS showed preliminary signals of earlier response and longer time to first relapse than sham stimulation. These exploratory findings require confirmation in larger trials.

records.title: Connectivity- and frequency-individualized accelerated intermittent theta burst stimulation in treatment-resistant depression: A randomized controlled trial.
records.abstract: Accelerated intermittent theta burst stimulation (aiTBS) is an effective neuromodulatory intervention for treatment resistant depression (TRD). aiTBS delivers repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation sessions over a compressed timeframe and can be individualized to specific locations using resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) to target pathological cortical networks or individualized in time using electroencephalography (EEG) to determine optimal participant-specific stimulation frequencies. In this randomized, placebo-controlled trial, we tested these forms of personalization against sham stimulation. Fifty-one patients with TRD were randomized to one of three arms; 43 completed the protocol per pre-specified criteria and assigned to one of three arms: (1) fMRI-connectivity-individualized aiTBS; (2) frequency- and connectivity-individualized aiTBS; or (3) sham aiTBS. Participants received 10 aiTBS sessions per day for five consecutive days with clinical assessments at baseline, and 1 and 4 weeks post-treatment. The primary outcome was change in depression severity on the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale from baseline to 1 week post-treatment. Anhedonia severity measured with the Dimensional Anhedonia Rating Scale was a secondary outcome. No significant differences were observed between active and sham arms on primary MADRS or secondary DARS endpoints for either the intent-to-treat or per-protocol sample. Remission and response rates also did not differ between arms. aiTBS individualized using either rs-fMRI or EEG and rs-fMRI failed to yield significant antidepressant benefits over sham stimulation, with relatively muted overall therapeutic benefits, underscoring the need for further clinical trials evaluating the efficacy of personalized aiTBS in TRD.

records.title: Psychological and neurobiological outcomes of combined rTMS and robotic therapy in post-stroke depression: A randomized controlled study.
records.abstract: This randomized controlled study evaluated the psychological, functional, and neurobiological effects of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) combined with intelligent robot-assisted rehabilitation in patients with post-stroke depression (PSD). Ninety eligible inpatients with PSD were randomized equally to an experimental group receiving 10-Hz rTMS plus robot-assisted rehabilitation and conventional rehabilitation, or to a control group receiving escitalopram plus conventional rehabilitation, for four weeks. Outcomes included depressive symptoms, functional independence, gait function, anxiety, social functioning, quality of life, and peripheral biomarkers including BDNF, cortisol, IL-6, and TNF-alpha. The experimental group showed greater improvement in HAMD and MBI scores after adjustment for baseline values, improved gait outcomes, and favorable within-group changes in anxiety, social-function, and quality-of-life measures. Biomarker analyses showed increased BDNF expression and decreased cortisol, IL-6, and TNF-alpha levels after treatment. These findings suggest that combined rTMS and intelligent robot-assisted rehabilitation is a feasible non-pharmacological intervention for PSD and may improve both psychological and functional outcomes, potentially through enhanced neuroplasticity and reduced inflammatory activity. Larger multicenter randomized trials with sham-control arms and longer follow-up are needed to confirm efficacy, durability, and mechanisms.

records.title: Comparative efficacy of neuromodulation techniques for Alzheimer's disease: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
records.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Neuromodulation techniques (NMTs) have shown potential therapeutic value in Alzheimer's disease (AD), but the comparative efficacy of different modalities remains unclear. This study aimed to systematically compare and rank available NMTs to identify their relative benefits across cognitive, functional, and neuropsychiatric outcomes.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate and rank the efficacy of NMTs in improving cognitive function, activities of daily living (ADLs), and neuropsychiatric symptoms in AD patients, thereby providing evidence-based guidance for clinical intervention strategies.
METHODS: English-language literature was systematically searched in PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and EMBASE from database inception to February 2026. Inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of AD patients aged ≥18 years. Interventions included repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS), transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), photobiomodulation (PBM), transcutaneous electrical stimulation (TES), transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS), transcranial pulse stimulation (TPS), deep brain stimulation (DBS), and sham stimulation (Sham). Outcome measures included Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), Alzheimer' s Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive Subscale (ADAS-Cog), Alzheimer' s Disease Cooperative Study-Activities of Daily Living (ADCS-ADL), Boston Naming Test (BNT), Neuropsychiatric Inventory (NPI), and Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS). Data extraction and risk-of-bias assessment followed Cochrane guidelines. Network meta-analysis (NMA) was conducted in Stata 17.0, with effect sizes ranked by the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA).
RESULTS: A total of 36 RCTs involving 1,445 patients were included in the analysis. Compared with Sham, TPS significantly improved MMSE (MD = 3.92, 95% CI: 1.57 to 6.35; SUCRA = 97.50%), MoCA (MD = 4.99, 95% CI: 2.26 to 7.72; SUCRA = 69.25%), and BNT scores (MD = 4.02, 95% CI: 1.81 to 6.23; SUCRA = 81.8%). rTMS also showed favorable effects on ADAS-Cog scores (MD = -11.10, 95% CI: -14.51 to -7.71; SUCRA = 91.00%). Regarding activities of daily living, TES ranked highest on the ADCS-ADL scale (SUCRA = 71.00%). In terms of neuropsychiatric symptoms, TPS achieved the highest ranking for improving NPI scores (SUCRA = 92.3%), whereas tACS showed the best performance on GDS scores (SUCRA = 69.5%).
CONCLUSION: Neuromodulation interventions demonstrated domain-specific benefits in AD, with no single approach showing universal superiority. TPS demonstrated the greatest potential for improving global cognitive outcomes, while rTMS showed advantages in ADAS-Cog performance. Nevertheless, limited sample sizes, heterogeneous stimulation protocols, and insufficient long-term evidence restrict the generalizability of current findings. Future multicenter RCTs with standardized protocols and prolonged follow-up are needed to confirm these results and guide clinical implementation.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: PROSPERO, CRD420261364193.

records.title: Efficacy of transcranial alternating current stimulation on cognitive function in patients with dementia: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
records.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) has shown potential for improving cognitive function in dementia, but evidence remains inconsistent. This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to evaluate the efficacy of tACS on cognitive function in dementia.
METHODS: We searched seven databases for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) assessing tACS effects on cognitive function in dementia. Two reviewers independently screened the literature, extracted data, and assessed study quality. A random-effects model was used to calculate standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). GRADE was used to rate evidence quality.
RESULTS: A total of 9 RCTs involving 357 patients with dementia were included. Compared with sham stimulation, tACS significantly improved immediate global cognition (SMD = 0.28; 95% CI [0.01, 0.54]; p = 0.04, I² = 39%), but not at follow-up. tACS also significantly improved immediate recall, delayed recall, and associative memory. Additionally, tACS significantly enhanced cholinergic transmission as measured by short-latency afferent inhibition (MD = 0.34, p < 0.001, I² = 0%). However, no significant effect was observed for neuropsychiatric symptoms, and the evidence for executive function was inconclusive. No serious adverse events occurred.
CONCLUSION: tACS may improve immediate global cognition and memory in patients with dementia, but no significant benefit was observed at follow-up or for neuropsychiatric symptoms. Findings are limited by few studies, heterogeneous parameters, and insufficient follow-up data. Future large, well-designed RCTs with standardized protocols are needed to optimize tACS parameters and confirm sustained efficacy.
records.journal: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology

records.title: The importance of power in photobiomodulation: a systematic review and meta-analysis of high-intensity laser therapy.
records.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Low-level laser therapy (LLLT; ≤ 0.5 W) is guideline-recommended in the United States for shallow-tissue oral mucositis and other superficial pathologies but has generally failed in trials for deeper tissue conditions due to limited penetration and subtherapeutic dosing. By contrast, Class IV high-intensity laser therapy (HILT; ≥ 0.5-80 W), typically at ∼100-fold higher power, has proven successful for many of these deeper tissue indications.
METHODS: We systematically searched PubMed, Google Scholar, and the Cochrane Database for Class IV HILT trials published from 2018 to April 2026, classifying interventions as effective when they showed large effect sizes (Cohen's d > 0.8).
RESULTS: Across 105 included studies (n = 2,710 HILT; n = 2,925 controls), no serious adverse events were reported. HILT reduced pain in all randomized trials of knee (k = 27), spine/neuromuscular (k = 20), shoulder/arm (k = 20), and wounds (k = 2), with > 90% showing large effect sizes. Additional benefits were observed in disorders of the feet (k = 13), hand/wrist (k = 8), face/jaw (k = 7), osteoporosis (k = 2), endometriosis, coronary artery disease, cognitive impairment, fibromyalgia, COVID-19, and obesity. HILT yielded durable analgesia, with large VAS pain reductions at end of treatment, < 3-month, and ≥ 3-month follow-ups (SMD -0.98, -1.18, and -1.01; k = 50, 19, and 21, respectively). Functional outcomes improved consistently, including range of motion (92%; k = 26), functional performance (84%; k = 57), and quality of life (85%; k = 25). Structural and physiological changes were observed, including increased knee cartilage thickness, reduced rotator cuff tear size, weight loss, and improved nerve conduction. Comparative trials showed HILT produced greater pain reduction than LLLT in 13/13 studies, all with large effect sizes. Mean HILT power was 9.3 W (median 10.0; range 0.5-30), and mean power density was 19.5 W/cm2 (median 10; range 0.1-52.5).
CONCLUSION: Class IV high-intensity laser therapy appears effective and safe for durable pain reduction across deep-tissue musculoskeletal pathologies, supporting its recognition in clinical practice and coverage by payers as a valuable therapeutic option. Further multicenter trials are needed to refine treatment protocols.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251021772, identifier CRD420251021772.

records.title: Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation targets the brain-gut axis to treat functional dyspepsia: a scoping review of clinical evidence and mechanistic research.
records.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Functional dyspepsia (FD) is a common gut-brain interaction disorder with suboptimal response to pharmacotherapy. Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS), a non-invasive neuromodulation targeting the vagus nerve, has emerged as a promising brain-gut axis therapy. This scoping review (PRISMA-ScR, JBI methodology) synthesizes clinical and preclinical mechanistic evidence on taVNS for FD.
METHODS: PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library were searched up to December 20, 2025, following PRISMA-ScR. Using PICOS (adults with FD; taVNS; sham/non-vagal/active controls; symptoms, gastric function, psychological outcomes, biomarkers; RCTs/clinical trials and controlled animal studies), two reviewers independently screened, extracted data, and assessed bias (RoB2 for RCTs, SYRCLE for animal studies). A narrative synthesis was performed due to heterogeneity.
RESULTS: Four RCTs (n = 480) and eight preclinical rodent studies met inclusion. All RCTs showed significant improvements in dyspeptic symptoms, gastric accommodation, slow-wave normalization, and comorbid anxiety, depression, sleep disturbance versus sham/non-vagal control, sustained for 4-12 weeks. Stimulation parameters varied (10-30 Hz; 0.5-10 mA; 2-4 weeks); risk of bias low-moderate. Preclinical rodent evidence supported five interconnected candidate mechanisms: (i) autonomic balance and cholinergic modulation; (ii) α7nAChR/NF-κB anti-inflammatory pathway with duodenal barrier restoration; (iii) NGF/TrkA/PLC-γ/TRPV1-mediated visceral hypersensitivity suppression; (iv) HPA axis inhibition; (v) rebalancing of brain-gut peptides (motilin, CCK, GLP-1).
CONCLUSION: This review characterizes taVNS as a safe, well-tolerated, mechanistically plausible non-invasive neuromodulation for FD acting on multiple brain-gut axis nodes. However, the small number of trials, parameter heterogeneity, and limited follow-up constrain definitive conclusions. Adequately powered, multicenter RCTs with standardized protocols and long-term follow-up are needed to confirm efficacy and define optimal regimens.

records.title: Cognitive performance and self-reported physical exercise in bipolar disorder: A cross-sectional analysis of pre-randomization screening data from an ongoing randomized controlled trial.
records.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Bipolar Disorder (BD) is frequently associated with persistent cognitive deficits that significantly impair functionality and quality of life. While physical exercise (PE) has shown promise in improving cognition in healthy individuals and those with other psychiatric conditions, most consistently in major depressive disorder and schizophrenia, its specific impact on individuals with BD remains under-investigated. This study aimed to investigate the association between self-reported regular physical exercise and cognitive performance in individuals with Bipolar Disorder.
METHODS: This study consists of a cross-sectional analysis of pre-randomization screening data from an ongoing randomized controlled trial. The analysis included 108 euthymic BD individuals (aged 18-55) recruited from the outpatient clinic at the University of São Paulo Medical School (PROMAN). Participants were allocated into either the Exercise Group (n = 48), defined by self-reported engagement in regular structured physical exercise at least twice a week, and the No-Exercise Group (n = 60); exercise status was ascertained with a brief in-house checklist. Cognitive performance was assessed using the Screen for Cognitive Impairment in Psychiatry (SCIP). Secondary measures included mood symptoms (MADRS and YMRS) and pharmacological treatment profiles. Effect sizes were estimated with Cohen's d, and a Bonferroni-corrected threshold of α = 0.0033 was applied to the 15 comparisons performed.
RESULTS: The Exercise group demonstrated significantly higher SCIP Total Scores compared to the No-Exercise group (64.63 ± 9.19 vs. 56.50 ± 7.84; p < 0.001, d = 0.95). Significant advantages for the exercise group were observed in sub-domains related to verbal learning (p = 0.010) and working memory (p = 0.002); the total score and working memory remained significant after Bonferroni correction, whereas verbal learning did not. Notably, the No-Exercise group had a significantly higher usage of stimulants (27.5% vs. 4.5%, p = 0.029), while the Exercise group had a higher prevalence of anticonvulsant use (45.5% vs. 20%, p = 0.035); neither medication difference survived correction.
LIMITATIONS: Exercise status was self-reported and dichotomous, with no data on intensity, duration or modality, and no demographic or clinical covariates were available for adjustment.
CONCLUSION: Regular physical exercise appears to be associated with superior global cognition, verbal learning, and working memory in individuals with BD. These findings, derived from the screening phase of an ongoing trial, suggest that PE may be a promising adjunctive strategy for neurocognitive rehabilitation, although the cross-sectional design precludes any causal inference.

records.title: Exercise to enhance antipsychotic effectiveness and mitigate metabolic harm: systematic review and meta-analysis.
records.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Antipsychotics are first-line treatments for schizophrenia and related psychotic disorders but are frequently accompanied by cardiometabolic adverse effects (weight gain, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, hyperglycaemia). We assessed whether supervised exercise interventions enhance psychopathology outcomes and reduce antipsychotic-related metabolic harm in adults receiving antipsychotic treatment medication.
DESIGN: Systematic review and meta-analysis.
DATA SOURCES: We searched PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus following PRISMA 2020 (PROSPERO CRD420251139904). Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) published since 2000 that tested supervised exercise in people receiving antipsychotics were eligible.
ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA FOR SELECTING STUDIES: Two reviewers selected studies using PICOS criteria, assessed methodological quality with the Revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomised trials (RoB 2), and pooled effects with random-effects models, expressed as mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The certainty of evidence was assessed with GRADE.
RESULTS: Twenty-eight studies (n = 1119) and four additional analyses met inclusion criteria. Exercise significantly improved negative symptoms (MD -3·078, 95% CI -4·457 to -1·699; p < 0·001), general psychopathology (-2·178, -4·140 to -0·216, p = 0·034), and PANSS total score (-7·069, -13·290 to -0·849; p = 0·030). Effects on positive symptoms were not significant (-1·220, -2·462 to 0·022; p = 0·053). Exercise reduced body weight (-1·620, -3·080 to -0·159; p = 0.034), body fat percentage (-1·250, -2·174 to -0·327; p = 0·020), and waist circumference (-1·420, -2·646 to -0·195; p = 0·032), with no material change in BMI. No significant effects were observed for systolic, diastolic blood pressure or fasting glucose. Lipid outcomes were largely null, with limited and inconsistent evidence, including a small increase in total cholesterol. Based on GRADE assessment, the certainty of evidence was moderate for negative symptoms, general psychopathology, body weight, body fat percentage, and waist circumference, with low to very low for the remaining outcomes.
CONCLUSION: Supervised exercise may be a beneficial adjunct to antipsychotic treatment, improving core psychopathology, particularly negative symptoms, and favourably shifting body composition by reducing adiposity and central fat, although the magnitude of change did not reach clinically meaningful thresholds. High-quality, adequately powered RCTs using multicomponent exercise and comprehensive metabolic endpoints are needed to determine effects on blood pressure, lipid profile, and glucose regulation.
FUNDING: None.

records.title: Lithium during maintenance electroconvulsive therapy: Secondary neuropsychological outcomes from the open-label PRASED randomized controlled trial.
records.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Lithium is commonly used for relapse prevention after successful electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). However, the combination of lithium and ECT has warranted caution in clinical practice due to concerns about cognitive tolerability, while evidence remains inconclusive.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the neuropsychological effects of maintenance ECT (M-ECT), with and without lithium, in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) across all ages.
METHODS: The Preventing Relapse After Successful Electroconvulsive therapy for Depression (PRASED) study was a multicenter, open-label, randomized controlled trial. Patients who achieved remission after an acute ECT course for MDD were randomized to receive symptom driven M-ECT and maintenance pharmacotherapy with or without adjunctive lithium. In this secondary outcome analysis, neuropsychological functioning was assessed repeatedly over six months using a comprehensive test battery covering global cognition, memory, attention, fluency, processing speed and subjective memory complaints. Linear mixed-effects models were applied to examine group differences in cognitive trajectories over time and associations between serum lithium levels and cognitive outcomes.
RESULTS: No significant differences in cognitive trajectories were observed between the lithium (n = 50) and non‑lithium (n = 46) group. Neuropsychological performance improved over time in both groups across all cognitive domains except verbal fluency. Serum lithium levels were not associated with neuropsychological performance.
CONCLUSION: Lithium addition during M-ECT was not associated with impaired objective or subjective neuropsychological functioning. These findings support the neuropsychological tolerability of concurrent lithium and ECT use in the maintenance phase and may help guide treatment decisions regarding relapse prevention following successful ECT.

records.title: [Tiaoshen acupuncture for shift work circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder: a randomized controlled trial].
records.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To observe the clinical efficacy of Tiaoshen (regulating the mind) acupuncture for shift work circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder (SWD).
METHODS: A total of 84 patients with shift work circadian rhythm SWD were randomly divided into a Tiaoshen acupuncture group (42 cases, 1 case dropped out) and a non-meridian non-acupoint group (42 cases, 2 cases dropped out). Both groups received sleep health education as basic treatment. The Tiaoshen acupuncture group was treated with Tiaoshen acupuncture, Baihui (GV20), bilateral Fengchi (GB20), Touwei (ST8), Shenmen (HT7), Zusanli (ST36), as well as auricular points Shenmen (TF4), Xin (CO15) were selected. The non-meridian non-acupoint group received shallow needling at non-meridian non-acupoint points, as well as non-related auricular points. Both groups were treated 3 times per week for 4 weeks. Before treatment, after treatment, and after 3 months of treatment completion, the morningness-eveningness questionnaire (MEQ), Pittsburgh sleep quality index (PSQI), self-rating anxiety scale (SAS), and self-rating depression scale (SDS) were used to assess the sleep and emotional status in the two groups.
RESULTS: Compared before treatment, the MEQ scores were increased after treatment and after 3 months of treatment completion in the two groups (P<0.001, P<0.01); the scores of PSQI, SAS and SDS were decreased after treatment and after 3 months of treatment completion in the Tiaoshen acupuncture group (P<0.001), and the scores of SAS and SDS were decreased after treatment in the non-meridian non-acupoint group (P<0.01). After treatment and after 3 months of treatment completion, the MEQ scores in the Tiaoshen acupuncture group were higher than those in the non-meridian non-acupoint group (P<0.001), and the PSQI scores in the Tiaoshen acupuncture group were lower than those in the non-meridian non-acupoint group (P<0.001); after treatment, the SAS and SDS scores in the Tiaoshen acupuncture group were lower than those in the non-meridian non-acupoint group (P<0.05, P<0.01).
CONCLUSION: Tiaoshen acupuncture can effectively improve the sleep-wake rhythm and sleep quality of patients with shift work circadian rhythm SWD, alleviate the accompanying anxiety and depression.
records.journal: Zhongguo zhen jiu = Chinese acupuncture & moxibustion

records.title: [Acupuncture regulates the Th17/Treg axis for chronic spontaneous urticaria: a randomized controlled trial].
records.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To observe the clinical efficacy of acupuncture for chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) and its effect on the helper T cell 17(Th17)/regulatory T cell (Treg) axis.
METHODS: Eighty CSU patients were randomly divided into an observation group (40 cases, 2 cases dropped out) and a control group (40 cases, 2 cases dropped out). The observation group received acupuncture at bilateral Jianyu (LI15), Shousanli (LI10), Quchi (LI11), Pianli (LI6), Xuehai (SP10), Zusanli (ST36) and Sanyinjiao (SP6), each session lasting for 30 min, 3 times per week. The control group received oral ebastine tablets, 10 mg each time, once daily. Both groups were treated for 8 weeks. The 7-day urticaria activity score (UAS7), dermatology life quality index (DLQI) score and Hamilton anxiety scale (HAMA) score were observed, peripheral blood Th17 and Treg cell proportions, and serum levels of interleukin (IL)-17, IL-23, IL-10, and IL-35 were detected, and the ratio of Th17/Treg was calculated before and after treatment in the two groups.
RESULTS: After treatment, the UAS7, DLQI and HAMA scores in the two groups were decreased compared with those before treatment (P<0.05), and the scores in the observation group were lower than those in the control group (P<0.05). After treatment, the peripheral blood Th17 cell proportions, the ratios of Th17/Treg and serum levels of IL-17, IL-23 in the two groups were decreased compared with those before treatment (P<0.05), those indexes in the observation group were lower than those in the control group (P<0.05). After treatment, the peripheral blood Treg cell proportions, and serum levels of IL-10, IL-35 in the two groups were increased compared with those before treatment (P<0.05), those indexes in the observation group were higher than those in the control group (P<0.05).
CONCLUSION: Acupuncture can effectively alleviate the symptoms of CSU, and its mechanism of action may be related to the regulation of the Th17/Treg axis.
records.journal: Zhongguo zhen jiu = Chinese acupuncture & moxibustion

records.title: Six-month supervised telerehabilitation combining pilates-based therapeutic exercise and self-myofascial release in adults with fibromyalgia: a randomized controlled trial.
records.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effects of a 6-month supervised multicomponent telerehabilitation programme combining Pilates-based therapeutic exercise and self-myofascial release on fibromyalgia impact, sleep quality, and psychological outcomes.
DESIGN: Two-arm, parallel-group randomized controlled trial.
SUBJECTS/PATIENTS: 68 adults with fibromyalgia confirmed according to the 2016 ACR criteria.
METHODS: Participants were randomized to a 6-month supervised home-based telerehabilitation programme (n = 35) or usual care (n = 33). The intervention comprised 3 live online sessions weekly combining Pilates-based therapeutic exercise, self-myofascial release, core stabilization, low-load resistance exercise, stretching, and relaxation. Outcomes were assessed at baseline, 3 months, and 6 months using validated patient-reported measures.
RESULTS: Significant group-by-time interactions were observed for fibromyalgia impact (p < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.132), sleep quality (p < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.129), depressive symptoms (p = 0.002, partial η2 = 0.129), and perceived stress (p = 0.028, partial η2 = 0.065), but not for anxiety (p = 0.701). Mean intervention adherence was 87.5%, with no adverse or serious adverse events reported in either group.
CONCLUSION: 6 months of supervised multicomponent telerehabilitation produced favourable longitudinal changes in fibromyalgia impact, sleep quality, depressive symptoms, and perceived stress compared with usual care.

records.title: Acupuncture for older adults with dementia in residential care homes: an assessor-blinded, randomised controlled trial.
records.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Dementia harms the mental health of older adults and poses a significant caregiver burden. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of acupuncture in managing cognitive decline and related symptoms in older adults with dementia.
METHODS: Eligible participants were recruited from 19 local residential care homes for older people in Hong Kong, China, from 5 October 2021 to 27 August 2024, in an assessor-blinded, randomised controlled trial. 118 participants were randomised to acupuncture and care-as-usual control (n=59 in each group) for 12 weeks. The analyses were on the intention-to-treat population. The primary outcome was the mean baseline-to-endpoint change of the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score. Secondary outcomes included the functional independence, pain, depressive and sleep symptoms.
RESULTS: 85.6% (101/118) of participants completed the study. The primary outcome, MoCA, was not significantly improved in week 12. Subgroup analyses showed that the treatment effect on MoCA appeared to differ across dementia severity strata. Acupuncture was superior over control in improving functional independence (the Chinese version of the Modified Barthel Index, mean difference=4.12, 95% confidence interval=0.81, 7.44, P=0.015; standardised effect size=0.29). All treatment-related adverse events were mild, and 2 nontreatment-related death cases were reported.
CONCLUSIONS: While no significant effect in cognitive function was observed, acupuncture was associated with an improvement in functional independence, and the treatment effect on cognition might differ across dementia severity strata. This warrants further validation of the exploratory results, identifying a subpopulation of older adults with dementia who could gain more benefits from acupuncture in improving cognitive function.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: www.ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04305951, date of registration: 10/03/2020.

records.title: Large-scale brain network modulation by auricular vagus neuromodulation in major depressive disorder: a systematic review of neuroimaging evidence.
records.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Auricular vagus neuromodulation, encompassing transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) and transcutaneous electrical cranial-auricular acupoint stimulation (TECAS), is an emerging noninvasive intervention for major depressive disorder (MDD). Neuroimaging studies of its central effects have expanded rapidly, yet findings remain dispersed across heterogeneous designs and have not been integrated at the cohort level.
METHODS: We followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines and searched five databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, Web of Science Core Collection, and PsycINFO) from inception to June 30, 2026; only English-language reports were included. Two reviewers independently screened records, extracted effect-level data, and appraised methodological quality using the 2024 JBI tool for quasi-experimental studies. Reports from the same cohort were identified via trial registrations, and denominators were counted once per cohort. Findings were stratified by five imaging paradigms and synthesized via cohort-level vote-counting, with null effects reported alongside positive findings.
RESULTS: Seventeen neuroimaging reports arose from nine independent cohorts (321 enrolled patients with MDD, 293 in imaging analyses, 144 healthy controls). The most reproducible finding was bidirectional normalization in striatal-cortical reward-circuit regions across four cohorts, qualified by null nucleus accumbens and putamen seed findings in one cohort. Default-mode-network regions were implicated in seven of nine cohorts, with heterogeneous directions. The only anterior insula effect surviving between-group correction was confined to an acute stimulation-state paradigm, and stimulation-state connectivity changes were frequency-band-specific. Twenty-seven of the coded effects were explicitly null. The sole machine-learning model (AUC = 0.856) was evaluated only by internal cross-validation. Quality appraisal rated two reports high, fourteen moderate, and one low.
CONCLUSION: The evidence remains strictly hypothesis-generating: auricular vagus neuromodulation is accompanied by distributed treatment-associated brain changes, but establishes neither causal pathways nor clinically actionable imaging markers. Confirmatory multi-center, sham-controlled trials with preregistered imaging endpoints, harmonized stimulation parameters, explicit null-result reporting, and independent external validation are needed.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261421762, identifier CRD420261421762.

records.title: Short-term Rhodiola rosea supplementation improves premenstrual symptoms, reaction time, and perceived exertion in female taekwondo athletes: a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial.
records.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Premenstrual symptoms may negatively influence psychological readiness, cognitive-motor performance, and perceived exertion in female athletes. Rhodiola rosea (RR) is an adaptogenic herb that has been investigated for its potential effects on fatigue, stress tolerance, mood, and exercise-related outcomes. However, its effects on premenstrual symptoms and performance-related responses in female athletes remain unclear. This study aimed to investigate the effects of short-term RR supplementation during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase on premenstrual symptoms, peripheral serum serotonin and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) concentrations, reaction time, perceived exertion, and aerobic performance-related indices in female taekwondo athletes with premenstrual syndrome (PMS).
METHODS: In this randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 24 female taekwondo athletes with moderate-to-severe PMS symptoms were randomly assigned to receive either 500 mg/day of standardised RR extract (n = 12) or placebo (n = 12) for 10 days during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase. Premenstrual symptoms were assessed using the Premenstrual Symptoms Screening Tool (PSST). Visual reaction time, peripheral serum serotonin and GABA concentrations, time to exhaustion (TTE), estimated VO₂max, and rating of perceived exertion (RPE) were evaluated before and after the intervention. Data were analysed using analysis of covariance with baseline values as covariates.
RESULTS: Compared with placebo, RR supplementation significantly reduced several PMS symptoms, including irritability, depression, anxiety, social withdrawal, decreased concentration, hypersomnia, food cravings, crying, skin problems, and abdominal pain (p < 0.05). The RR group demonstrated faster reaction time compared with placebo (adjusted mean difference: -60 ms; p < 0.001). Peripheral serum serotonin and GABA concentrations were significantly higher in the RR group than in the placebo group (p < 0.001). In addition, RR supplementation reduced post-exercise RPE (adjusted mean difference: -1.40 Borg units; p = 0.006). However, no significant differences were observed between groups in TTE or estimated VO₂max (p > 0.05).
CONCLUSION: Short-term RR supplementation during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase may improve selected PMS symptoms, visual reaction time, and perceived exertion in female taekwondo athletes with PMS. Larger trials with hormonal confirmation of menstrual cycle phase, longer intervention periods, direct physiological measurements, and sport-specific performance assessments are required to confirm these findings.
records.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

records.title: Transcranial alternating current stimulation for major depressive disorder: An updated systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials with GRADE assessment.
records.abstract:
PURPOSE: Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) may modulate neural oscillations implicated in major depressive disorder (MDD). This systematic review and meta-analysis assessed the efficacy, follow-up effects, tolerability, and safety of tACS in adults with MDD.
METHODS: PubMed/MEDLINE, CENTRAL, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and Embase were searched from inception to March 29, 2026, for randomized controlled trials of active tACS in adults with MDD. Primary analyses compared active tACS with sham or inactive control, while active-protocol comparisons were analyzed separately. Random-effects models were used to calculate pooled mean differences (MDs) or odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Heterogeneity was assessed using I2, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach.
RESULTS: Eleven reports from nine randomized trials were included. Active tACS did not significantly reduce clinician-rated depressive symptom severity compared with control (8 studies, 471 participants; MD -1.80, 95% CI -4.80 to 1.20; I2 = 89.8%), indicating substantial heterogeneity. However, tACS was associated with higher odds of treatment response (8 studies, 680 participants; OR 2.41, 95% CI 1.28-4.56; I2 = 62.1%) and remission (4 studies, 270 participants; OR 4.69, 95% CI 2.37-9.28; I2 = 30.1%). A significant effect was also observed for response at the latest reported assessment (7 studies, 608 participants; OR 2.70, 95% CI 1.62-4.49; I2 = 20.3%). Regarding safety, active tACS increased the likelihood of at least one adverse event (3 studies, 475 participants; OR 1.95, 95% CI 1.12-3.41), while estimates for headache and cutaneous symptoms were imprecise and not significantly different between groups. Overall certainty of evidence ranged from very low to moderate.
CONCLUSION: tACS may improve response and remission rates in MDD, but its effect on mean symptom severity remains uncertain. High heterogeneity and limited data for protocol-specific subgroup analyses reduce interpretability, as pooled estimates reflect heterogeneous stimulation parameters rather than specific regimens. Given the small evidence base and limited certainty, routine clinical use cannot be recommended. Well-powered, standardized, and independently conducted trials with longer follow-up are required.

records.title: Body weight following a multidomain lifestyle intervention in older adults at risk of dementia - A post-hoc analysis of the AgeWell.de-trial.
records.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Lifestyle interventions provide a promising approach to address higher body weight as a risk factor for dementia.
OBJECTIVE: The AgeWell.de-trial was primarily designed to preserve cognitive function and reduce dementia risk. In this post-hoc analysis, we investigated body weight following the multidomain intervention among older adults with overweight or obesity, as well as the role of motivation and confidence regarding weight loss.
METHODS: Analyses used data from the cluster-randomized AgeWell.de-trial, testing a multidomain intervention (dietary counselling, enhancement of physical, social and cognitive activity, medication review, intervention for cardiovascular risk factors, depressive symptoms/grief, if applicable) over 24 months in adults aged 60 to 77 years at risk for dementia. Associations between intervention allocation and body weight at follow-up were analyzed using linear regression, controlling for covariates, based on multiply imputed data.
RESULTS: The sample included n = 678 participants with a BMI ≥ 25 kg/m², mean age (SD): 68.9 (4.8), 52.1% female. Group allocation was not associated with body weight at 24-month follow-up (b (unstandardized regression coefficient) = -0.30, 95% CI: -0.51; 1.11). Older age (b = -0.14, 95% CI: -0.25; -0.03) and a high level of education (b = -1.28, 95% CI: -2.55; 0.00) were linked to lower body weight at follow-up, while higher baseline body weight predicted higher body weight at follow-up (b = 0.95, 95% CI: 0.91; 0.98). Levels of motivation and confidence regarding weight loss remained high but stable in both groups, regardless of group allocation.
CONCLUSIONS: In this post-hoc analysis, group allocation was not associated with lower body weight at follow-up. Despite high levels of motivation and confidence regarding weight loss and favorable changes in diet and physical activity in the intervention group, these changes did not translate into measurable weight loss.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: AgeWell.de was prospectively registered in the German Clinical Trials Register on December 7th, 2017 (DRKS trial identifier DRKS00013555).

records.title: Acupuncture combined with auriculotherapy as adjunctive therapy for hyperemesis gravidarum: A randomized controlled trial evaluating hospital stay, relapse rate, and quality of life.
records.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the efficacy of acupuncture combined with auricular therapy as an adjunct to standard fluid resuscitation in patients with hyperemesis gravidarum (HG).
METHODS: A total of 122 HG patients were randomly assigned to the acupuncture combined (AC) group (n = 61) or standard fluid (SF) group (n = 61). The SF group received conventional fluid replacement alone, while the AC group received acupuncture and auricular therapy in addition to fluid resuscitation. Primary outcomes included the Pregnancy-Unique Quantification of Emesis and Nausea (PUQE) score, the Functional Living Index-Emesis (FLIE) score (total and subscores), serum potassium, length of hospital stay, and recurrence frequency; secondary outcomes included the Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS) and Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS) scores. Within-group changes and between-group differences were analyzed using paired t-tests and analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) or Mann-Whitney U tests, respectively.
RESULTS: Both groups exhibited significant within-group improvements in PUQE, FLIE, nausea, vomiting, SAS and SDS scores (all p < 0.001), with no meaningful change in serum potassium. Post-treatment between-group comparisons, assessed by analysis of covariance adjusted for baseline values, showed significant advantages for adjuvant acupuncture combined with auriculotherapy in total FLIE score (adjusted mean difference -4.11, 95%CI -8.15 to -0.07, p = 0.046), nausea subscore (adjusted mean difference -2.11, 95%CI -4.01 to -0.22, p = 0.029), SAS (adjusted mean difference -1.04, 95%CI -2.07 to -0.01, p = 0.049) and SDS (adjusted mean difference -1.61, 95%CI -3.12 to -0.10, p = 0.037), but no significant differences in PUQE, vomiting subscore or serum potassium. The AC group had a shorter median hospital stay (4 vs 6 days, p = 0.041) and lower recurrence frequency (0.15 ± 0.441 vs 0.39 ± 0.759, p = 0.048). The proportion of participants with recurrence was 11.48% in the AC group and 24.59% in the SF group, with no significant difference (p = 0.068).
CONCLUSION: While standard fluid resuscitation effectively relieves the core symptoms of HG, adjunctive acupuncture combined with auriculotherapy provided additional benefits regarding quality of life, psychological status, hospital stay, and recurrence frequency, although no significant intergroup difference was observed in post-treatment PUQE scores or the proportion of patients experiencing HG recurrence. This combined intervention may serve as a safe and valuable adjunctive strategy for HG management. Further sham-controlled trials are required to distinguish specific treatment effects from non-specific contextual factors.

records.title: Home Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation With Gamified Cognitive Control Training for Depression: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
records.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) has emerged as a home-based treatment in major depressive disorder (MDD), although its effects are typically small to moderate and inconsistently observed. Because tDCS may act synergistically with behavioral interventions, combining both approaches represents a promising strategy for developing more effective home-based treatments for MDD.
OBJECTIVE: To investigate the feasibility, safety, and efficacy of home-based tDCS and concurrent gamified cognitive control training (CCT) in adults with MDD.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This multicenter, double-masked, parallel-group, randomized clinical trial with follow-up at week 10, masking checks at 2 time points, and expectancy assessments was conducted at 3 university hospitals in Latvia, Germany, and Israel between June 22, 2021, and August 8, 2024. Participants included adults aged 18 to 65 years with MDD, 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores of at least 13, and no or stable antidepressant medication.
INTERVENTION: Participants were randomly assigned 1:1 to active tDCS (2 mA; anode F3, cathode F4) plus a gamified CCT or sham tDCS plus a sham game. Participants were asked to complete 30 home treatment sessions (30 minutes each) over 6 weeks with software-assisted electrode positioning.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was feasibility, defined as completing at least 20 of 30 sessions with greater than 50% probability. The secondary outcome was efficacy, measured as change in Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) scores from baseline to week 6.
RESULTS: Of 111 enrolled participants, 109 were included in the modified intention-to-treat sample (55 in the active group and 54 in the control group; mean [SD] age, 33.1 [10.6] years; 69 female [63.3%]). Feasibility criteria were met, with 86 participants (78.9%) completing at least 20 sessions (lower bound of 1-sided 95% CI, 71.5%). The MADRS scores improved significantly in both groups at week 6, indicating insufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis of no difference in the mean change in MADRS score from baseline to 6 weeks between the 2 treatment groups (difference, 0.89 [95% CI, -1.37 to 3.15]; P = .44; Cohen d, 0.10 [95% CI, -0.15 to 0.34]). Results were similar at follow-up (week 10). Adverse events were balanced between groups.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: This RCT of home-based tDCS combined with CCT in adults with MDD was feasible and safe but did not demonstrate superior efficacy over the control condition. Future studies should refine the mechanistic alignment between stimulation and cognitive interventions to optimize treatment effects.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04953208.

records.title: Right putaminal gray matter change tracks psychomotor recovery after accelerated iTBS in melancholic treatment-resistant depression.
records.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Psychomotor retardation is a prominent and disabling feature of melancholic depression. Accelerated intermittent theta-burst stimulation (aiTBS) may hasten antidepressant effects, but neural substrates of early symptom improvement remain unclear. Given the central role of frontostriatal circuitry in motivation and behavioral activation, structural alterations in the striatum may represent a possible neural substrate of early therapeutic change.
METHODS: Structural MRI was acquired from 61 patients with melancholic TRD and 77 healthy controls, and voxel-based morphometry was used to assess baseline striatal gray matter volume differences. Patients then underwent a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial of left dorsolateral prefrontal aiTBS, comprising 20 sessions over four days. In 50 patients with complete pre- and post-treatment data, we tested whether GMV change in the baseline-identified striatal region was associated with clinical change in the active and sham groups (n = 25 each).
RESULTS: Patients showed greater right putamen GMV than controls at baseline. After active aiTBS, greater right putamen GMV increase was associated with greater psychomotor retardation improvement. This association was absent after sham stimulation and was not observed for overall depression severity.
CONCLUSION: The right putamen appears structurally altered in melancholic TRD. After active aiTBS, short-term putamen GMV increase was associated with psychomotor rather than broader depressive improvement. This pattern should not be interpreted as structural normalization but may reflect a relationship between putaminal change and early psychomotor recovery.

records.title: Altered GABAB receptor sensitivity in heavy drinkers indexed using a TMS-based biomarker: a randomized controlled experimental medicine trial.
records.abstract: Metabotropic γ-aminobutyric acid type B receptors (GABABRs) are implicated in alcohol use disorder (AUD) and represent a promising therapeutic target. However, robust biomarkers of GABABRs target engagement and sensitivity in humans are lacking. We examined transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS)-derived cortical inhibition and growth hormone (GH) release as measures of GABABR function, and whether heavy alcohol use is associated with altered responses to pharmacological GABABR activation. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study, 31 healthy volunteers (16 heavy drinkers, 15 light drinkers) received baclofen 30 mg, baclofen 60 mg, or placebo across three sessions. Long-interval intracortical inhibition (LICI), short-interval intracortical inhibition, and intracortical facilitation were assessed with paired-pulse TMS at baseline and ~60 min post-dose. Baclofen blood concentrations and plasma GH levels were measured. Baclofen produced dose-dependent increases in GH release, confirming neuroendocrine GABABR engagement. The LICI response to baclofen differed between groups: In light drinkers, baclofen at 30 mg potentiated LICI, and a similar potentiation was seen at 60 mg, indicating that a plateau may have been reached. In contrast, in heavy drinkers, a potentiation of LICI similar to that in light drinkers was seen at 30 mg baclofen, but was absent at the 60 mg dose despite comparable pharmacokinetics, suggesting altered GABABR function. Effects were selective for GABABR-mediated inhibition, with no consistent modulation of short-interval intracortical inhibition or corticospinal excitability. Acute baclofen administration reveals altered GABABR sensitivity in heavy drinkers, with preserved responses at lower doses but reduced response under stronger agonist stimulation. LICI and GH release provide complementary biomarkers of central and peripheral GABABRs engagement and may support translational development of mechanism-based treatments for AUD.

records.title: Effects of E-Coach-Based Chronic Disease Management on Self-Management, Quality of Life, and Mental Health in Maintenance Hemodialysis Patients.
records.abstract: The study investigated the effects of E-Coach on self-management behavior, quality of life (QoL), and mental health of patients with maintenance hemodialysis (MHD). The study included 96 patients receiving regular MHD, and they were randomly assigned to receive either usual care (a UC group) or usual care plus E-Coach intervention (an E-Coach group). The E-Coach was implemented through a WeChat-based mini-application that provided health education, dietary and exercise guidance, medication reminders, and regular online counseling through text-based materials, videos, and interactive quizzes. After adjustment for baseline score, the self-management behavior score after 6 months remained significantly higher in the E-Coach group than in the UC group (analysis of covariance (ANCOVA): F(1, 93) = 6.3, p = 0.014, partial η2 = 0.06), with a mean difference of +11.6 (95%CI: 9.7 to 13.6; p < 0.001 by Bonferroni correction). The mean self-management behavior score increased from 57.1 to 78.3 points in the E-Coach group, representing a change of +21.2 points, compared with a change of +7.9 points (from 58.6 to 66.5 points) in the UC group. The between-group difference in change was +13.3 (95%CI: 9.9 to 16.5). As for the Kidney Disease Quality of Life-Short Form, the magnitude of score increase from baseline to 6 months was higher in the E-Coach group than the UC group, suggesting an improvement in patients' QoL. Regarding the Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS) and Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS), the E-Coach group had a greater magnitude of score reduction from baseline to 6 months compared to the UC group, indicating a reduction in depressive and anxiety symptoms. The E-Coach group exhibited lower levels of potassium and phosphorus after 6 months than the UC group. The study demonstrates the superior effectiveness of E-Coach in enhancing self-management behavior, improving QoL, and alleviating depressive and anxiety symptoms in patients receiving MHD.

records.title: Rapid and robust effects of high-dose intermittent Transcranial Brain Stimulation (iTBS) on depression and suicidal ideation in adolescents with acute major depression: a 10-day randomised, controlled, single-blind trial.
records.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Depression is extremely common among adolescents and can significantly increase the risk of suicide when severe. High-dose intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS) is a secure and efficacious physical treatment. However, clinical evidence in adolescents remains limited. This research is designed to assess the therapeutic impacts of high-dose iTBS on depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, and suicidal ideation in adolescents suffering from acute depression, along with the factors linked to treatment response.
METHODS: A total of 61 patients were randomly assigned to either the high-dose iTBS group or the sham stimulation group. All participants received 10 daily sessions of high dose iTBS stimulation over a two-week period, targeting the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). Outcome measures assessed at baseline, post-intervention, and 1-month follow-up included 24-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD-24) scores, Beck Scale for Suicide Ideation - Chinese Version (BSI-CV), and Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAMA). Clinical factors influencing iTBS efficacy were further analyzed.
RESULT: At the end of the 10-day intervention, the high-dose iTBS group exhibited significantly lower HAMD-24 (p = 0.008, Cohen`s d = 0.71 [95%CI: 0.188-1.224]) and BSI-CV (p = 0.011, Cohen`s d = 0.67[95%CI: 0.154-1.186]) scores compared with the sham group, and this advantage persisted at the 1-month follow-up (Week 6) (HAMD-24: Cohen`s d = 0.96[ 95%CI: 0.43-1.49]; BSI-CV: Cohen`s d = 0.76[95%CI: 0.24-1.28]). In contrast, between-group differences in HAMA scores were non-significant both post-intervention (Week 2) and at the 1-month follow-up (Week 6) (p > 0.05). Moreover, poorer family functioning within the high-dose iTBS cohort was associated with diminished therapeutic benefit (p < 0.05).
CONCLUSION: Current research indicates that a 10-day course of high-dose iTBS is effective in alleviating depressive symptoms and suicidal ideation in adolescents with depression, and that the therapeutic effects persist for up to one month after the end of treatment. We also found that high-dose iTBS was less effective in patients with poor baseline family functioning.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: Chinese clinical trial Registry (ChiCTR2500101152), trial registration date: April 21, 2025(retrospectively registered).

records.title: Combining Cognitive Training and Brain Stimulation: A Novel Approach to Address Disordered Eating and Antipsychotic-Induced Weight Gain in People With Severe Mental Illness.
records.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Antipsychotic-induced weight gain is a distressing side effect that most often occurs within the first 3-6 months of pharmacological initiation, significantly increasing cardiometabolic risk and mortality in individuals with severe mental illness.
AIMS: To assess the feasibility of reducing food craving and binge eating using Approach Bias Modification Training (ABMT) combined with real or sham Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation (tDCS).
METHOD: In this double-blind, parallel-group, two-arm, sham-controlled trial, adults with schizophrenia/schizoaffective disorder on stable doses of antipsychotics were randomly allocated to a total of five ABMT sessions together with either real or sham tDCS administered over 3 weeks. Assessments were made at baseline (T0), post-treatment (T1) and at a 2-week follow-up (T2). Feasibility outcomes included recruitment, attendance, retention, tDCS safety, acceptability, tolerability, and blinding. Secondary outcomes were changes in food craving, binge eating, approach bias to food, body mass index, and psychological symptoms.
RESULTS: Twenty-eight participants were recruited (93% of target). Retention was high (T1 = 85.7% and T2 = 78.6%); blinding accuracy was 46.4%. Medium effect sizes favoured 'ABMT + real tDCS' for reducing binge eating (d = -0.6, 95% CI -1.5, 0.3), and 'ABMT + sham tDCS' for reducing food cravings (d = 0.5, 95% CI -0.4, 1.4). Within-groups, only the 'ABMT + real tDCS' arm showed reduced approach bias to food and approach-avoidance bias to food, and increased avoidance bias to food (all p < 0.05). This was followed by reduced binge eating episodes (p < 0.05). Both groups reported frequent binge-eating episodes ('ABMT + tDCS' = 43%; 'ABMT + sham tDCS' = 28.6%).
CONCLUSION: The initiation of antipsychotic therapy is a critical clinical window for early intervention to mitigate the long-term metabolic and psychiatric consequences of antipsychotic-induced weight gain. Combining ABMT + tDCS is acceptable and may help reduce binge eating in individuals on antipsychotics, with a potential synergistic effect between cognitive training and brain stimulation. A confirmatory trial is needed to assess its effectiveness and should include BED diagnosis as a stratification criterion.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ISRCTN Identifier: 13280178.

records.title: Cerebellar Continuous Theta Burst Stimulation for Insomnia Disorder: A Randomized Sham-Controlled Trial.
records.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effects of cerebellar continuous theta burst stimulation (cTBS) in insomnia disorder (ID).
METHODS: In this randomized sham-controlled trial, patients with ID received 2 weeks of active or sham cerebellar cTBS. The primary outcome was a ≥ 3-point improvement in Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) score after treatment. Secondary outcomes included changes in sleep, mood, and resting-state fMRI.
RESULTS: Seventy-two patients (51 women; mean age, 44.3 ± 11.6 years) were included in the intention-to-treat analysis. More patients in the active than sham group achieved a ≥ 3-point PSQI improvement after treatment (75.0% vs. 33.3%; adjusted OR, 6.06; 95% CI, 2.17-18.50; p < 0.001). Active cTBS reduced PSQI scores versus sham both post-treatment (adjusted mean difference, -3.34; 95% CI, -4.57 to -2.12; p < 0.001) and at 1 month (-3.70; 95% CI, -4.93 to -2.48; p < 0.001), and also improved Insomnia Severity Index, Hamilton Anxiety Scale, and Hamilton Depression Scale at both time points (all p < 0.01). Exploratory fMRI analyses identified several post-treatment connectivity differences between groups, but only right amygdala-right orbitofrontal connectivity showed a significant group-by-time interaction (FDR-adjusted p = 0.038). No serious adverse events occurred.
CONCLUSION: Cerebellar cTBS was well tolerated and promising for ID.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05992285).

records.title: Electroacupuncture Combined with Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia Alleviates Insomnia-Anxiety Comorbidity in Gynecological Cancer Patients Undergoing Chemotherapy: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
records.abstract: Insomnia and anxiety affect many gynecological cancer patients on chemotherapy, and non-pharmacological options are limited. This randomized trial examined whether adding electroacupuncture (EA) to cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) improves both conditions. Seventy-six patients received EA + CBT-I or sham EA + CBT-I for 4 weeks. Outcomes included sleep quality (PSQI), insomnia severity (AIS), anxiety (HAMA), objective sleep parameters, and overall response rate. At Week 4, the EA group showed a greater reduction in PSQI global score (mean difference in change from baseline: -3.11, 95% CI: -4.11 to -2.11, p < 0.001). More patients in the EA group achieved AIS ≤ 6 (71.1% vs. 42.1%, p = 0.010) and HAMA ≤ 14 (92.1% vs. 65.8%, p = 0.005). Deep sleep (p = 0.001), REM sleep (p = 0.045), and sleep score (p = 0.008) also increased more with EA group. The overall response rate was higher with EA (92.1% vs. 71.1%, p = 0.016). No serious adverse events occurred. These findings suggest that adding EA to CBT-I improves sleep and anxiety in this population, with a favorable safety profile.

records.title: Efficacy of Personalizing Cognitive Remediation for Schizophrenia by Targeting Impairments in Early Auditory Processing.
records.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND HYPOTHESES: Early auditory processing (EAP) deficits are common but not universal in schizophrenia, are linked to impairments in higher cognitive functions and when improved are associated with downstream cognitive improvements. Assessment of baseline EAP training need provides an opportunity for cognitive remediation (CR) programs to personalize treatment and optimize impact. This confirmatory efficacy study examined the differential benefit of EAP training for those with and without baseline EAP deficits. Hypotheses were: (1) Only EAP impaired (EAP-) patients would benefit more from CR that included EAP training, (2) cognitive gains made by EAP- patients during CR that included EAP training would mediate the relationship between gains in EAP and functional capacity.
STUDY DESIGN: 184 outpatient adults diagnosed with schizophrenia were classified as having intact (n = 91) or impaired (n = 81) EAP and randomized to CR with restorative exercise plans that either included EAP training (n = 89) or did not (n = 83). Cognitive and functional outcomes were measured post-treatment and 3 months later.
STUDY RESULTS: Across CR treatment conditions, cognitive gain effect size was moderate. Treatment condition did not significantly impact EAP, cognitive, or functional outcomes for either EAP group at final endpoint. EAP improved significantly but modestly for EAP- patients across conditions. Cognitive gains did not mediate the relationship between EAP gains and functional capacity.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings support the value of CR for people with schizophrenia, demonstrate that EAP deficits are malleable, and that cognitive and functional gains can occur for EAP impaired patients, regardless of whether EAP training is provided.

records.title: Transcranial alternating current stimulation as psychiatric intervention: A meta-analytic primer.
records.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) is an emerging neuromodulation approach targeting neural oscillations. Although mechanistic studies support its neurophysiological effects, clinical evidence across psychiatric symptoms remains limited. This transdiagnostic meta-analysis provides a quantitative assessment of tACS effects across psychiatric symptom domains and identifies areas of clinical promise.
METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized sham-controlled trials assessing tACS in adults with psychiatric conditions was conducted. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and CENTRAL were searched until August 2026. Standardized mean differences (Hedges' g) were calculated using random-effects models, with exploratory analyses investigating clinical and methodological moderators.
RESULTS: Eighteen studies (19 datasets; 1045 participants) were included. Compared with sham stimulation, tACS showed a moderate overall effect (SMD = -0.41, 95% CI [-0.60, -0.2], I2 = 72%). The strongest significant findings were observed for depressive symptoms (n = 10; SMD = -0.44, 95% CI -0.76 to -0.01) and anxiety symptoms (n = 4; SMD = -0.64, 95% CI -1.12 to -0.17, I2 = 62%). Significant improvements were also observed for obsessive-compulsive symptoms, inattention, and post-traumatic stress symptoms, although based on limited evidence. Exploratory analyses identified preliminary patterns across stimulation frequencies and symptom domains, including significant effects of gamma-frequency stimulation on depressive symptoms.
CONCLUSION: This transdiagnostic meta-analysis identifies early therapeutic signals of tACS across psychiatric symptoms, with the most consistent evidence observed for depressive symptoms. Frequency-specific effects may influence clinical outcomes and warrant further investigation to optimize stimulation parameters.

records.title: Effects of primary somatosensory cortex high-definition transcranial direct current stimulation combined with core stability training on pain and glutamate levels and neuromuscular function in chronic low back pain: a randomized controlled trial.
records.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chronic low back pain (CLBP) involves pain-related changes in sensory processing, motor control, and broader neurobiological function. The primary somatosensory cortex (S1) is a relevant neuromodulation target because it contributes to sensory-discriminative pain processing and exhibits maladaptive plasticity in chronic pain states. However, S1-targeted high-definition transcranial direct current stimulation (HD-tDCS) has been insufficiently studied in CLBP.
OBJECTIVE: To determine whether S1-targeted HD-tDCS combined with core stability training reduces pain intensity and pain-related disability in adults with CLBP, and to explore associated changes in paraspinal muscle biomechanical properties, resting-state EEG activity, and serum metabolites.
METHODS: In this randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial, 36 adults with CLBP received active or sham S1 HD-tDCS combined with a standardized 4-week core stability training program. Pain-related scale was assessed using the VAS, ODI, RMDQ and FABQ. Secondary outcomes included biomechanical properties of the lumbar erector spinae and multifidus measured using MyotonPRO. Exploratory outcomes included resting-state electroencephalographic alpha-band power spectral density (PSD) and phase-locking value (PLV) connectivity, as well as untargeted serum metabolomics in a subset of participants.
RESULTS: Compared with sham stimulation, active S1 HD-tDCS was associated with greater reductions in VAS, ODI, RMDQ and FABQ scores after treatment. The active group also showed larger decreases in lumbar erector spinae and multifidus tone and stiffness, along with greater improvement in elasticity. Resting-state EEG demonstrated increased alpha-band PSD across frontal, central, and parieto-occipital regions and reduced alpha-band PLV connectivity after active stimulation. In the metabolomics subset, active treatment was associated with greater reductions in circulating L-glutamate and enrichment of ferroptosis-related pathways. Changes in pain intensity were correlated with changes in paraspinal muscle stiffness, central alpha-band PSD, and L-glutamate levels.
CONCLUSIONS: S1-targeted HD-tDCS combined with core stability training may improve short-term pain intensity and pain-related disability in adults with CLBP. The accompanying muscular, electrophysiological, and metabolomic findings were consistent with the clinical changes. These findings support S1-targeted HD-tDCS as a potential adjunct to exercise-based rehabilitation in CLBP.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR2300076620 (Registration date 2023-10-13).

records.title: Feasibility and tolerability of combining 6 Hz transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) at 3.2 mA and digital cognitive training in older adults with mild cognitive impairment.
records.abstract:
PURPOSE: Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) may enhance cognition and potentiate digital cognitive training (DCT) in mild cognitive impairment (MCI). Optimal intensity remains uncertain because higher currents may increase cortical electric fields but raise tolerability concerns. We evaluated feasibility and tolerability of 3.2 mA tACS plus DCT, and exploratorily assessed active versus sham effects on inhibitory control and cognitive transfer.
METHODS: Ten older adults with MCI received five daily 6-Hz tACS sessions over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex during DCT; ten sham-arm participants from a randomized trial completed identical DCT. Feasibility and tolerability were assessed by adherence, attrition, and side-effect monitoring. Exploratory efficacy used repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni-corrected paired comparisons. Outcomes included antisaccade total errors, verbal and visual memory, and visuoconstructive abilities.
RESULTS: All participants completed treatment (100% adherence). Active-session side effects were mild in 67% and moderate in 23%; no severe events occurred. Side-effect burden was unrelated to DCT performance (p = 0.22). Antisaccade total errors showed a group × time interaction (p = 0.028), favoring active stimulation. Reaction time showed no stimulation-specific effects. Verbal and visual memory showed time effects (p = 0.016 and p = 0.002), whereas visuoconstructive abilities showed a trend-level group × time interaction favoring active stimulation (p = 0.054).
CONCLUSIONS: Higher-intensity tACS plus DCT was feasible and well tolerated in older adults with MCI. Exploratory findings suggest that active stimulation may improve inhibitory control and facilitate transfer to selected cognitive domains. Confirmation in the ongoing randomized controlled trial is warranted.

records.title: The Effect of Exercise Training on Individuals With Osteoporotic Vertebral Fracture: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
records.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Osteoporotic vertebral fractures significantly impair physical function and quality of life; however, evidence regarding the long-term effects of exercise interventions remains inconclusive. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of exercise training on pain, quality of life, physical performance, depression, kinesiophobia, and sleep quality in individuals with osteoporotic vertebral fractures.
METHODS: In this single-centre, open-label randomized controlled trial (unblinded), 48 participants with osteoporotic vertebral fractures were randomly allocated (1:1) to an intervention group (n = 24) or a control group (n = 24). Forty-four participants (intervention: 23, control: 21) completed the study. The intervention group received individually supervised, 40-minute exercise sessions twice weekly for 12 weeks, focusing on spinal extensor, postural, lower-extremity strengthening, and balance exercises. Resistance progressed from body weight to external resistance based on individual tolerance, and balance tasks progressed from static to dynamic, with missed sessions rescheduled within the same week. The control group continued usual activities. Pain was assessed using the Short Form McGill Pain Scale, quality of life with the QUALEFFO-41 questionnaire, physical performance with the 6-minute walk test, depression with the Beck Depression Scale (BDS), disability with the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), and kinesiophobia with the Tampa Kinesiophobia Scale (TKS). Sleep quality and sleepiness were evaluated using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS).
RESULTS: Compared with the control group, the intervention group demonstrated significantly greater improvements in VAS pain (mean difference: -1.24, 95% CI: -1.59 to -0.89; p < 0.05) and 6-minute walk distance (38.94 m, 95% CI: 29.59 to 48.28; p < 0.05). Significant improvements favoring the intervention group were also observed for depression (BDS: -4.52, 95% CI: -6.51 to -2.54; p < 0.05), disability (ODI: -2.63, 95% CI: -4.13 to -1.12; p < 0.05), and kinesiophobia (TKS: -10.81, 95% CI: -13.50 to -8.12; p < 0.05) as well as the QUALEFFO-41 total score (p < 0.05). No statistically significant between-group differences were found for sleep quality (PSQI; p = 0.057) or daytime sleepiness (ESS; p = 0.210).
DISCUSSION: A 12-week structured exercise program appears to provide superior benefits in reducing pain and improving functional capacity, depression, and kinesiophobia compared with usual care. These findings suggest that such exercise protocols can be effectively integrated into rehabilitation plans for participants with osteoporotic vertebral fractures, though some elements such as sleep quality may require further investigation.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05521724 (Registered: August 24, 2022). Ethical approval: Hasan Kalyoncu University Ethics Committee (Approval No: 2021/011; February 17, 2021).

records.title: [Effects of biofeedback electrical stimulation integrated with Chinese medicine emotional care on alleviating symptoms in the patients with chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome].
records.abstract: Objective To evaluate the efficacy of biofeedback electrical stimulation combined with Chinese medicine emotional nursing in improving symptoms among patients with chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CP/CPPS). Methods Seventy patients who met the inclusion criteria of CP/CPPS were randomly divided into the conventional group and the combined intervention group, with 35 cases in each group. The control group received oral tamsulosin sustained-release capsules along with routine care. In addition to the conventional treatment, the patients in combined intervention group received biofeedback electrical stimulation combined with Chinese Medicine emotional nursing. Biofeedback electrical stimulation was administered three times per week for a total of 8 weeks. The National Institutes of Health Chronic Prostatitis Symptom Index (NIH-CPSI), International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS), Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAMA), and Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD) were used to assess patients at baseline, 4 weeks, and 8 weeks of intervention. Results No significant differences in baseline data were observed between the two groups before the intervention (P>0.05). After 4 and 8 weeks of intervention, both groups showed significant improvements in NIH-CPSI, IPSS, HAMA and HAMD scores compared to baseline (P<0.05). Compared to the control group, the combined intervention group demonstrated significantly greater reductions in the total NIH-CPSI score, its pain subscore, IPSS score, and HAMA score at both 4 and 8 weeks (P<0.05). By the 8th week, the combined intervention group also showed a significantly greater reduction in the NIH-CPSI urination subscore and HAMD score (P<0.05). However, no statistically significant intergroup difference was found in the NIH-CPSI quality of life subscore (P>0.05). Furthermore, the combined intervention group achieved significantly higher rates of nursing satisfaction (97.05%) and overall efficacy (91.18%) compared to the control group (P<0.05). Conclusion The combined intervention of biofeedback electrical stimulation and Chinese Medicine emotional nursing can significantly alleviate urinary symptoms, pelvic pain, and anxiety-depression moods in patients with CP/CPPS. Although there was no statistically significant difference in the quality of life scores between the two groups, the combined intervention may provide potential benefits for the long-term improvement of patients' quality of life in terms of the improvement of core clinical symptoms and emotional states.

records.title: Efficacy and safety of theta-burst stimulation for obsessive-compulsive disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
records.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a prevalent psychiatric disorder characterized by intrusive obsessions and repetitive, compulsive behaviors that are difficult to inhibit. Several studies have evaluated the efficacy of theta-burst stimulation (TBS) for alleviating OCD symptoms, reporting potential outcomes in both symptom reduction and functional improvement. This study aimed to synthesize evidence from published randomized clinical trials (RCTs) regarding the clinical effectiveness of TBS in patients with OCD.
METHODS: We searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Embase databases. A total of eight RCTs and one open-label study were included, each comparing TBS with sham stimulation in relation to the severity of obsessive and compulsive symptoms. The primary measure was the Yale-Brown Obsessive-Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) between two groups from baseline to the endpoint (immediate effect) and from baseline to the end of follow-up period (long-term effect). The secondary outcome was depressive symptoms reported by The Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAM-D). Continuous outcomes were pooled as mean differences (MDs), while the dichotomous outcomes were pooled as risk ratios (RRs).
RESULTS: This review included eight RCTs and one open-label study, comprising a total of 305 patients. According to the immediate action of TBS, it showed significant improvement in only the obsession sub-scale (MD = -1.04, 95%CI [-1.87, -0.22], p = 0.01, I2= 0%). While according to the long-term action, TBS showed significant improvement in 'obsession' sub-scale (MD = -1.63, 95%CI [-2.81, -0.44], p = 0.007, I² = 31%) and 'compulsion' sub-scale (MD = -1.68, 95%CI [-2.57, -0.8], p = 0.0002, I² = 0%), respectively. Also, it showed a significant reduction of HAM-D (MD = -2.16, 95%CI [ -3.89, -0.43], p = 0.01, I2 = 15%).
CONCLUSION: The results showed that TBS could be effective as an adjunctive treatment for OCD in relieving the obsessive-compulsive symptoms, especially the long-term action with well-tolerated adverse effects.

records.title: Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation in perioperative neurocognitive disorders: clinical evidence and mechanistic perspectives.
records.abstract:
